summary: Gathers use cases and requirements for provisioning data that helps SIP service providers route sessions, focusing on a "registry" element. DRINKS stands for Data for Reachability of Inter-/Intra-NetworK SIP. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Phone companies need a shared address book to find where to send calls. This describes how entries get put into that address book, and what the address book must be able to do.

questions: how do sip providers exchange routing data
what is a registry in sip routing
subtitle: Requirements for provisioning SIP routing data into a shared registry

tldr.problem: SIP service providers need to exchange routing information (where to send calls) with each other and internally. Doing this via bilateral negotiations between every pair of providers does not scale; a shared registry would be more efficient.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines use cases and requirements for a registry system that SIP providers can provision with telephone number ranges, public identifiers, and routing information. Local data repositories then use this registry to route calls.
tldr.outcome: A common registry for SIP routing data enables efficient interconnection between carriers and simplifies call routing management, though the actual provisioning protocol specification is left to future work.

facts.label: Session Establishment Data components
facts.value: Ingress point, protocol, IP address, port, and routing rules

facts.label: Public identifier types
facts.value: Telephone numbers, SIP addresses, globally routable URIs

facts.label: Registry hierarchy levels
facts.value: Data Recipient, Route Group, Destination Group, Public Identifier

today: RFC 6461 is Informational and represents a requirements document for future protocol work. It has not been obsoleted. The actual provisioning protocols (IETF DRINKS) have since been specified in separate RFCs, but this document remains the authoritative source for the use cases and requirements that those protocols satisfy.

sections.title: SIP Routing and Session Establishment Data
sections.content:
Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is the standard for VoIP calls. When a SIP service provider (SSP) receives a call request for a phone number it does not serve, it must route the call to another provider. The routing information needed is called Session Establishment Data (SED), which includes things like the ingress point (where to send the call), the protocol (UDP, TCP, TLS), IP addresses, and ports.

Historically, two providers would establish a bilateral peering relationship and manually exchange SED. As the number of SIP providers grew, the number of required bilateral relationships became unmanageable. A DRINKS registry serves as a central clearinghouse: providers provision their SED into the registry, and other providers download what they need for routing. The actual data distribution to local repositories is out of scope for this RFC; the focus is on provisioning data into the registry.
sections.eli5: When you call someone through a phone company, that company needs to know where to send the call if the person is not their customer. A registry is like a shared phonebook where all the phone companies write down how to reach each other's customers.

sections.title: Registry Architecture and Data Organization
sections.content:
The RFC defines a hierarchical data model for organizing SED in a registry. At the top level, a Data Recipient is an entity (usually a provider) that needs routing information. A Route Group is a set of SED records associated with one or more Destination Groups. A Destination Group aggregates public identifiers (phone numbers, SIP addresses, etc.), telephone number ranges, or routing numbers that share common SED.

This hierarchy allows efficient management and targeted distribution: rather than provisioning SED record by record, an operator can group related identifiers and associate them with a route group, then distribute that group to specific recipients. A single provider or a third party can act as a Registrar to add, modify, and delete data in the registry on behalf of an SSP.
sections.eli5: The registry organizes phone numbers and routing info into groups. Phone Company A might say 'all these numbers belong to my customers, send calls here.' The registry then tells Phone Company B where to find Company A's customers.

sections.title: Interconnection and Provisioning Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC organizes its use cases into categories. Provisioning mechanisms cover real-time provisioning (immediate updates when a new customer signs up) and non-real-time bulk provisioning (nightly batch updates). Interconnect schemes address inter-SSP routing (between providers), direct peering (to a provider's own customers), and indirect peering (to another provider's customers via that provider). Intra-SSP SED allows a provider to maintain separate routing for internal calls versus external calls.

Other use cases cover selective peering (applying different routing policies to different peers), data validation (ensuring the registry data is consistent and accurate), and transfer of registry control between operators. The RFC also covers public identifier management, including telephone number ranges and routing numbers used in North America.
sections.eli5: Phone companies need to add customers in real time or in batch at night. They need to talk to other carriers, or directly to their own customers, or indirectly through partners. They might have different rules for different partners.

sections.title: Registry Requirements and Protocol Design Implications
sections.content:
The RFC translates use cases into formal requirements. The provisioning protocol must support adding, modifying, and deleting data in the registry, with transactional semantics (a set of operations either all succeed or all fail atomically). It must validate data before storing it and detect duplicate entries. The protocol should support authorization controls so that registrars can only modify data they are authorized for, and data recipients can only see data they are authorized to receive.

The requirements also address data consistency, retention policies, and conflict resolution when multiple registrars make conflicting updates. The RFC specifies that the protocol itself will be defined in future work, leaving this document to gather requirements and use cases from the industry.
sections.eli5: The protocol needs to add or change phone numbers in the registry, make sure the data is right, keep secrets, and handle conflicts if two phone companies try to update the same number at the same time.
